client: I've been really struggling lately with this huge group project I got assigned at university. The moment my professor announced it, I felt this wave of panic wash over me because I know it's going to involve a presentation in front of the whole class, and public speaking is basically my worst nightmare. I'm not even sure talking about it here is going to change anything, because the project is still going to be there when I leave this room.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a lot of anxiety about this project, and that fear of public speaking feels very real and overwhelming right now. I also notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's a part of you that's already questioning whether being here can help — and that kind of hopelessness can sometimes be its own barrier worth exploring. What would it mean for you if we *could* find some ways to make this feel more manageable — even just a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: I mean... I guess it would be a relief, but honestly I've tried things before and they haven't really stuck, so I'm not sure how this is any different. The presentation is in three weeks and just thinking about standing up there in front of everyone makes my chest tight right now, even just talking about it. I want to believe something could help, but part of me is already bracing for disappointment, you know?
therapist: That tension you're describing — wanting relief but protecting yourself from another disappointment — makes a lot of sense given what you've been through before. I'm curious, when you say things haven't "stuck," what did those attempts look like, and what do you think got in the way? Understanding that might actually help us figure out what could work differently this time.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Honestly, I've tried a few things over the years to deal with the loneliness — joining a community group once, downloading those social apps, even forcing myself to go to a neighbor's gathering — but I'd show up and just feel like I was performing, like nobody was really seeing me. And then I'd come home feeling even more hollow than before, which made me wonder why I bothered. I think what got in the way was that I kept waiting to feel some kind of real connection, and when it didn't happen fast enough, I just... retreated, told myself it wasn't worth it.
therapist: It's striking that even as you're describing feeling hollow and like it wasn't worth it, you're speaking quite quickly — like there's a lot of energy or urgency behind these memories, even if the feelings themselves feel flat or defeated. What you're describing — showing up, hoping for connection, and leaving feeling more alone — sounds genuinely painful, and it makes sense that you'd start to protect yourself by pulling back. I'm wondering, when you say nobody was really *seeing* you, what would it have looked like if someone had?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That's a hard question to answer, honestly. I think... if someone had really seen me, they would have noticed that I was quiet in the corner and actually come over, not just waited for me to perform being okay or make myself easy to talk to. Like, they would have been curious about me without me having to earn it first.
therapist: What you just described — being seen without having to earn it first — sounds like something really deep and important to you, almost like a longing that's been with you for a long time. And the way you said it, softly and carefully, makes me wonder if even putting that into words just now felt a little vulnerable. Does that wish — to be approached, to be curious about *without* having to perform — show up in how you're feeling about the presentation too?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Yeah, it does show up there. With the presentation, I keep thinking that if I mess up even one part of it, people will decide that's who I am — like one stumble erases everything else. And I guess what I want is for someone to wonder about me before I've even proven anything, but I don't really know how to let that happen without feeling like I'm just... waiting to be rejected.
therapist: That belief — that one stumble could define you entirely in other people's eyes — is such a heavy thing to carry into a room, and it sounds like it's been shaping how safe you feel letting people in for a long time. What's worth gently noticing is that the very thing you're longing for, being seen before you've proven anything, is actually something you're offering yourself very little of too. What do you think it would take to start being a little more curious about yourself, the way you wish others would be?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: That question kind of stopped me for a second, because I don't think anyone's ever put it that way before. Like, I'm sitting here wanting people to give me the benefit of the doubt, but I'm probably the harshest judge of myself in the room. I guess I'm just not sure what "being curious about myself" even looks like in practice, because it sounds nice but I honestly don't know where I'd start without it just turning into more self-criticism.
therapist: The fact that this question stopped you — that it landed differently — tells me something important is shifting, even if it feels uncertain right now. Being curious about yourself doesn't have to mean deep reflection; it can start as small as noticing a moment where you were harder on yourself than you would be on a friend, and just pausing to ask *why*. Would you be willing to try that this week — just noticing, without needing to fix anything yet?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: I guess I can try that... just noticing, not fixing. But honestly, my worry is that I'll notice something and then just spiral into feeling worse about myself, like I'll catch myself being harsh and then beat myself up for being harsh, you know? It feels like it could turn into another loop of guilt instead of actually helping.
therapist: That worry makes complete sense, and it's actually a really important thing to name — the inner critic is so practiced that it can even hijack the act of self-compassion. So let's build in a safeguard: when you notice harshness, the next step isn't to evaluate it, it's just to say to yourself, *"there it is"* — the same quiet curiosity you'd have watching a cloud pass, not a problem to solve. Does that feel like a version you could try without it becoming another thing to get right?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I like the idea of just saying "there it is" — it feels less loaded than trying to fix something. But honestly, even as you described it, I noticed this little voice going "okay, but am I doing the cloud thing right?" which kind of proves your point, I guess. It's like my brain is so wired to grade everything that I can't even practice not grading without grading the practice.
therapist: The fact that you caught that voice *in the moment* and could even laugh a little at it — that's not failure, that's actually the skill working. You just noticed something without letting it stop you, which means part of you already knows how to do this. What if "am I doing it right?" is just another cloud to say "there it is" to?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I mean... okay, yeah, when you put it that way it kind of makes sense. But there's still this part of me that worries if I just "notice" everything and let it pass, I'm not actually dealing with anything — like I'm just floating above my life instead of fixing what's actually wrong. What if the loneliness isn't just a thought, what if it's a real thing that needs a real solution, not just something to observe?
therapist: You're raising something really important — noticing isn't meant to replace action, it's meant to make sure the actions you take come from a clearer place rather than from panic or self-punishment. The loneliness is real, and it does need real connection — but what we're building here is the inner steadiness that might let you actually stay in those moments of connection instead of retreating when it gets hard. What do you think has made it difficult to stay, rather than just show up?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think what makes it hard to stay is that the moment I feel like someone might actually see me, I kind of... panic and pull back. Like there's this voice that says they'll eventually realize I'm too much, or not enough, or just exhausting to be around. And then I start acting weird or distant, and the connection just fades, which honestly feels like proof that I was right to be scared in the first place.
therapist: What you just described is such a clear example of a self-fulfilling prophecy — the fear of being "too much" actually creates the distance that then feels like confirmation of the fear, but the distance was never really proof, it was protection. I'm also noticing you shared something quite vulnerable just now in a way that felt almost matter-of-fact, like you've made a kind of peace with this pattern even though it's clearly still painful. What would it feel like to stay in one of those moments of potential connection — even for just a little longer than usual — before the voice gets to decide what happens next?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech
